## Getting Started (November 11, 2026)

Ava,

Your research question asks how Cook County officials in 1885–87 used financial and bureaucratic language to frame the poor and the institutionalized, and how that language worked as social control. So far you've read a handful of pages from the *Journal of the Proceedings of the Board of Commissioners of Cook County* closely. In this workspace, you will turn the **whole volume** into data, so you can test your argument across hundreds of pages instead of five. By the time you push this back to GitHub, you will have:

1.  **A page-by-page dataset of the volume**: one row per page, with its text and the date of the meeting it records.
2.  **Every page tagged by institution**: the Infirmary, the Insane Asylum, the County Hospital, the County Agent, and the Committee on Public Charities. This lets you keep the poorhouse and the asylum apart, or decide to treat them together, with evidence.
3.  **Counts of the two vocabularies your argument is about**, financial and medical, by institution and by month, plus **every use of key words in context** so you can read the counts back into the text.
4.  **A comparison** with the 1886 State Commissioners' investigation of the asylum, an outside voice describing the same institution in the same years.

Read the explanation before you run each chunk. The steps run in order, so each chunk needs the ones before it.

## 3. Unzip the volume

HathiTrust gives you the volume as a `.zip` file with **one text file per scanned page**. Each file holds the OCR text (the machine reading) of that page. `unzip()` extracts them into `data/cole/pages/`.

```{r}
#| label: unzip

# find the zip file I sent you in data/cole/raw/
zip_file <- list.files(rawdir, pattern = "\\.zip$", full.names = TRUE)
zip_file   # should show exactly one file

# unzip it into the pages folder, but only the first time (when no .txt pages are there yet)
if (length(list.files(pagedir, pattern = "\\.txt$", recursive = TRUE)) == 0) {
  unzip(zip_file[1], exdir = pagedir)
}

# list every page file, with its full path
page_files <- list.files(pagedir, pattern = "\\.txt$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE)
length(page_files)   # how many pages?
head(basename(page_files))  # the first few file names
```

Look at the file names. HathiTrust numbers each scan in order (its **sequence number**). This is **not** the page number printed on the paper: the scans include the cover, blank pages, and the title page, so scan 29 might be printed page 17. In this workspace, pages are identified by their sequence number (`seq`). When you need the printed page number for a citation, open the scan on HathiTrust by adding its sequence number to the end of this link, and read the number off the page: `https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015073344494&seq=`

## 4. Read the pages into a table

The loop below reads each page file and stores it as one row: the sequence number (taken from the last number in the file name) and the full text of the page.

```{r}
#| label: read-pages

# Start with an empty table: one column for the page number, one for its text
pages <- tibble(seq = integer(), text = character())

for (file in page_files) {
  # go through the page files one at a time
  seq_number <- as.integer(
  # turn the result into a number
    str_extract(basename(file),
                # file name only, without the folders
                "\\d+(?=\\.txt$)")) 
                # the digits that come right before ".txt"
  page_text  <- read_file(file) 
  # read the whole page into one piece of text
  pages <- bind_rows(pages, 
                     # add a row to the table:
                     tibble(seq = seq_number, text = page_text))
                     # this page's number and its text
}

pages <- pages %>% arrange(seq)   # put the pages in page order (see note)

nrow(pages)       # how many pages were read
pages$text[30]    # read the 30th page; change the number to read other pages
```

### Find the meeting dates

The *Proceedings* record the Board's meetings in order, and each meeting starts with its date ("Monday, January 10, 1887"). We find the first full date on each page. Pages without a date belong to the meeting that started on an earlier page, so `fill()` copies the last date found down to them.

```{r}
#| label: dates

# A regular expression list: any one of the twelve month names
month_names <- "January|February|March|April|May|June|July|August|September|October|November|December"

# The full date pattern, e.g. "March 3, 1887" or "March 3 1887"
date_pattern <- paste0("(", month_names, ")",  # a month name
                       "\\s+",         # one or more spaces (or a line break)
                       "\\d{1,2}",    # a day: one or two digits
                       ",?",          # an optional comma
                       "\\s+",        # one or more spaces
                       "18\\d\\d")     # a year from 1800 to 1899

pages <- pages %>%
  mutate(date_text = str_extract(text, date_pattern),   
         # the first date found on each page, or NA if none
         date = as.Date(str_remove(date_text, ","),    
                        # drop the comma: "March 3 1887"
                        format = "%B %d %Y")) %>%       
                        # %B = full month name, %d = day, %Y = 4-digit year
  fill(date, .direction = "down") %>%                   
  # a page with no date gets the date from the page above it
  mutate(month = format(date, "%Y-%m"))                 
  # turn the date into a "1887-03" label for grouping

pages %>% count(month)   # how many pages fall in each month
```

Some dates on a page belong to a contract, a bill, or a report covering an earlier month, not to the meeting itself. Skim the `date_text` column for pages where the date jumps backward, and treat the `month` column as approximate.

## 5. Clean the OCR

Before counting words, we fix two common OCR problems:

- **Hyphenated line breaks.** A word split across lines ("ex-\npenses") would be counted as two half-words. We rejoin it.
- **Mostly-number pages.** Financial statements and bills are long tables of numbers. They matter to your argument, but their OCR is mostly digits, so we flag them with `share_digits`, the share of characters that are digits.

```{r}
#| label: clean

# clean the OCR text and flag pages that are mostly tables of numbers
pages <- pages %>%
  mutate(
    # "chari-" + line break + "ties" becomes "charities"
    clean_text   = str_replace_all(text, "(\\w)-\\s*\\n\\s*(\\w)", "\\1\\2"),  # rejoin hyphenated words
    clean_text   = str_squish(clean_text),  # collapse runs of spaces and line breaks into single spaces
    n_chars      = str_length(clean_text),  # number of characters on the page
    share_digits = str_count(clean_text, "\\d") / pmax(n_chars, 1),  # share of characters that are digits (pmax avoids dividing by 0 on empty pages)
    table_page   = share_digits > 0.3  # TRUE if more than 30% digits: probably a table
  )

pages %>% count(table_page)  # how many pages look like tables
```

Save the page table. This CSV is your main dataset.

```{r}
#| label: save-pages

# save one row per page, without the raw OCR text (write_excel_csv keeps the text readable in Excel)
write_excel_csv(pages %>% select(seq, date, month, table_page, share_digits, clean_text),
                file.path(datadir, "proceedings-pages.csv"))
```

## 6. Which institution is on the page?

Your Historical Context feedback asked you to keep the **Infirmary** (the poorhouse) and the **Insane Asylum** apart, or to explain why you treat them together. Here we tag each page with every institution it mentions. A page can mention several.

`regex(..., ignore_case = TRUE)` makes the search ignore capital letters. The patterns allow for small variations: `(on|of)` matches "Committee on Public Charities" and "Committee of Public Charities".

```{r}
#| label: institutions

# one row per institution: its name, and a pattern that finds it (| means "or"; " ?" means an optional space)
institution_patterns <- tribble(
  ~institution,                   ~pattern,
  "Infirmary",                    "infirmary|poor ?house|alms ?house",
  "Insane Asylum",                "insane asylum|hospital for the insane",
  "County Hospital",              "county hospital",
  "County Agent",                 "county agent",
  "Committee on Public Charities","committee (on|of) public charities"
)

# an empty table to collect which pages mention which institution
page_institutions <- tibble(seq = integer(), institution = character())

# for each institution, find the pages that mention it
for (i in seq_len(nrow(institution_patterns))) {
  matches <- pages %>%  # start from all pages
    # keep pages that match this institution's pattern, ignoring capitals
    filter(str_detect(clean_text, regex(institution_patterns$pattern[i], ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%
    transmute(seq, institution = institution_patterns$institution[i])  # keep the page number, labelled with the institution
  page_institutions <- bind_rows(page_institutions, matches)  # add these pages to the collection
}

page_institutions %>% count(institution, sort = TRUE)  # pages per institution (a page can mention several)
```

How many pages mention **both** the Infirmary and the Insane Asylum? Try `page_institutions %>% count(seq) %>% filter(n > 1)`. Read two of those pages: are the two institutions discussed together, or just listed side by side?

## 7. Your two vocabularies

Your argument is that officials described the institutions in financial and bureaucratic terms rather than medical ones. Here you turn that argument into a test, by writing down **which words count as which**.

Choosing these words is an interpretive decision. "Care," for example, might be medical ("care of the sick") or administrative ("in the care of the Warden"). Start with the lists below, then add, remove, and justify. The lists are saved to `data/cole/word-lists.csv` so your choices are documented.

Now split every page into words, keep only the words on your lists, and count them by month. We count **per 1,000 words** because months with longer meetings print more pages and would otherwise always look bigger.

```{r}
#| label: count-vocab

# split every page into words: one row per word, with its page and month
page_words <- pages %>%
  select(seq, month, clean_text) %>%
  unnest_tokens(word, clean_text)  # also lowercases the words and drops punctuation

words_per_month <- page_words %>% count(month, name = "total_words")  # all words per month, to turn counts into rates

# count the words from each list per month, then per 1,000 words
vocab_by_month <- page_words %>%
  inner_join(word_lists, by = "word") %>%  # keep only words that are on one of the lists
  count(month, vocabulary) %>%  # list words per month and vocabulary
  left_join(words_per_month, by = "month") %>%  # add that month's total word count
  mutate(per_1000 = n / total_words * 1000)  # a rate, so months with more pages don't look bigger

vocab_by_month
```

```{r}
#| label: vocab-plot
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5

ggplot(vocab_by_month, aes(x = month, y = per_1000, fill = vocabulary)) +  # months across, rate up, one color per list
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +  # bars side by side, not stacked
  # titles and labels
  labs(title = "Financial and medical vocabulary in the Board's Proceedings",
       subtitle = "Words from each list per 1,000 words, by month (approximate)",
       x = NULL, y = "Per 1,000 words", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +  # a plain background
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))  # tilt the month labels so they don't overlap
```

```{r}

ggsave(file.path(outdir, "vocabulary-by-month.png"), width = 9, height = 4.5)
```

## 8. Read the counts back into the text: keywords in context

`keyword_in_context()` finds every use of a word and shows the words around it, like the "Contexts" tool in Voyant.

```{r}
#| label: kwic-function

# find every use of a keyword and return the text around it ("keyword in context");
# window = how many characters to keep on each side
keyword_in_context <- function(pages, keyword, window = 60) {
  results <- tibble(seq = integer(), month = character(), context = character())  # an empty table for the results
  pattern <- regex(paste0("\\b", keyword, "\\b"), ignore_case = TRUE)  # the keyword as a whole word (\b = word edge), ignoring capitals

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(pages))) {  # go through the pages one at a time
    text <- pages$clean_text[i]  # this page's text
    positions <- str_locate_all(text, pattern)[[1]]  # start and end of every match on this page
    for (j in seq_len(nrow(positions))) {  # for each match on the page
      start <- max(1, positions[j, "start"] - window)  # start `window` characters before it (but not before the page starts)
      end   <- min(str_length(text), positions[j, "end"] + window)  # end `window` characters after it (but not after the page ends)
      results <- bind_rows(results, tibble(seq = pages$seq[i],  # add a row: page, month, and the passage
                                           month = pages$month[i],
                                           context = str_sub(text, start, end)))
    }
  }
  results  # return the collected passages
}
```

Try it with words that name the people in these institutions:

```{r}
#| label: kwic-examples

inmate_contexts <- keyword_in_context(pages, "inmates")  # every use of "inmates", with 60 characters on each side
nrow(inmate_contexts)  # how many times it appears
head(inmate_contexts$context, 10)  # read the first 10 passages
```

```{r}
bodies_contexts <- keyword_in_context(pages, "bodies")  # the same for "bodies"
bodies_contexts %>% select(seq, month, context)  # page, month, and passage
```

```{r}
# save both sets of passages to data/cole/
write_excel_csv(inmate_contexts, file.path(datadir, "kwic-inmates.csv"))
write_excel_csv(bodies_contexts, file.path(datadir, "kwic-bodies.csv"))
```

Run `keyword_in_context()` for "patients," "paupers," "insane," and "economy." Who gets called a *patient*, and who an *inmate* or a *pauper*? Does it depend on the institution? Copy two or three revealing contexts into your notes with their sequence numbers, then look up their printed page numbers on HathiTrust. They are evidence you can quote.

## 9. An outside voice: the 1886 State report

The State Commissioners' 1886 report investigated the same asylum, in the same years, from outside the County Board. It was prompted by Dr. J. G. Kiernan's public criticism in October 1885. Does it use the same vocabulary?

```{r}
#| label: state-report

# read the State report and clean it the same way as the Proceedings
state_text <- read_file(state_report_file) %>%
  str_replace_all("(\\w)-\\s*\\n\\s*(\\w)", "\\1\\2") %>%  # rejoin hyphenated words
  str_squish()  # collapse extra spaces and line breaks

state_words <- tibble(text = state_text) %>% unnest_tokens(word, text)  # split it into words: one row per word

# rates of each vocabulary in the two sources, per 1,000 words
compare_vocab <- bind_rows(
  page_words  %>% mutate(source = "County Board Proceedings") %>% select(source, word),  # County words, labelled
  state_words %>% mutate(source = "State Commissioners' report, 1886")  # State words, labelled
) %>%
  group_by(source) %>%
  mutate(total_words = n()) %>%  # total words in each source
  ungroup() %>%
  inner_join(word_lists, by = "word") %>%  # keep only list words
  count(source, vocabulary, total_words) %>%  # list words per source and vocabulary
  mutate(per_1000 = n / total_words * 1000)  # per 1,000 words, so the longer source doesn't win by size

compare_vocab %>% select(source, vocabulary, n, per_1000)
```

The State report is about 21 pages; the *Proceedings* volume is hundreds. That's why we compare rates per 1,000 words, not raw counts. Even so, a short text gives noisy rates, so read the report itself before drawing conclusions.

## 10. Check your work

Before you use this data in your project:

- [ ] **Page count.** `nrow(pages)` should equal the number of scans in the volume on HathiTrust.
- [ ] **Landmarks.** The pages you already know turn up where they should. `pages %>% filter(str_detect(clean_text, "Aldrich")) %>% select(seq, month)` should include the scans of Aldrich's address (printed pp. 392–398), and `report_pages` (in the optional section) should include the scan of p. 133 with the "Disposition of bodies." Check both on HathiTrust.
- [ ] **Spot-check the tags.** Open five pages tagged "Insane Asylum" and five tagged "Infirmary." Is each tag right?
- [ ] **Spot-check OCR.** Compare three pages' `clean_text` with the scans on HathiTrust. Are your list words read correctly?
- [ ] **Commit.** This `.qmd` file, the CSV files in `data/cole/`, and everything in `output/cole/` are committed. `data/cole/raw/` and `data/cole/pages/` are not.

## Thinking like a historian about this pipeline

Every step here **transforms the source**.

- **These are the officials' words.** Everything in this dataset was written or approved by the Board, its committees, or its employees. You've already noticed the patients' silence and the data inherits it.

- **The printed record was political.** The Proceedings were published in years of public scandal, from the 1885-86 investigation to the 1887 "boodle" trials. Talk of "waste" and "abuses" can be reform rhetoric aimed at voters as much as a way of managing the poor.

- **Your word lists are an argument.** The result depends on which words you chose. The ones I have here are only suggestions. Report your lists and your reasons, and test whether the result holds when you add or remove a few words.

- **OCR reads tables badly.** Financial statements, bills, and monthly census tables are where much of the financial language lives, and they are where OCR makes the most mistakes. Give extra caution when reading pages flagged `table_page`.

- **Categories are evidence too.** "Inmate," "pauper," "patient," "insane": the labels officials used are part of your question, not neutral descriptions to adopt.

### Check your "n"s

> **Peng:** Count things, and compare the counts with *landmarks*: numbers you know should be true. If you expect 1,000 people and find 20, something's wrong. ([Peng, "Check your 'n's"](https://bookdown.org/rdpeng/exdata/exploratory-data-analysis-checklist.html#check-your-ns))

```{r}
#| label: eda-ns

pages %>% count(month)  # pages per month

# in how many different months does each institution appear?
page_institutions %>%
  left_join(pages %>% select(seq, month), by = "seq") %>%  # add each page's month
  distinct(institution, month) %>%  # one row per institution and month
  count(institution, name = "months_with_pages")  # count the months
```

### A first experiment: what words are distinctive of each institution?

```{r}
#| label: eda-tfidf
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

# the 10 words most distinctive of each institution's pages
distinctive <- page_words %>%
  inner_join(page_institutions, by = "seq", relationship = "many-to-many") %>%  # attach institutions to words by page
  anti_join(stop_words, by = "word") %>%  # drop common words like "the" and "of"
  filter(!str_detect(word, "\\d"), str_length(word) >= 3) %>%  # drop numbers and very short words (often OCR noise)
  count(institution, word) %>%  # how often each word appears with each institution
  bind_tf_idf(word, institution, n) %>%  # high for words common on one institution's pages but rare on the others'
  group_by(institution) %>%
  slice_max(tf_idf, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%  # keep the top 10 per institution
  ungroup()

distinctive %>%
  mutate(word = reorder_within(word, tf_idf, institution)) %>%  # order the bars within each panel
  ggplot(aes(x = tf_idf, y = word)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey40") +  # one bar per word
  scale_y_reordered() +  # needed with reorder_within()
  facet_wrap(~ institution, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +  # one panel per institution
  labs(title = "Words most distinctive of each institution's pages (tf-idf)",
       x = "tf-idf", y = NULL)
```

Do any of these words belong on your financial or medical lists? Are there words that suggest a third vocabulary you hadn't considered, such as discipline, labor, or morality? Write down two or three ideas.

## Optional: the monthly reports as a second dataset

The Infirmary's and asylum's monthly reports, like the "Disposition of bodies" on p. 133, are small tables: deaths, discharges, and where bodies went (Rush Medical College, Hahnemann, Northwestern Dental, burial). Turning them into a dataset would let you count what the officials' language describes.

OCR scrambles tables, so the most reliable way is to **transcribe them by hand** into a spreadsheet. With roughly two years of monthly reports, that's a few hours of careful work. Find the pages first:

```{r}
#| label: find-monthly-reports

# find the pages with the monthly reports on where bodies went
report_pages <- pages %>%
  filter(str_detect(clean_text, regex("disposition of bodies", ignore_case = TRUE))) %>%  # pages that mention "disposition of bodies"
  select(seq, month)  # keep page number and month

report_pages
```

Then create a spreadsheet with these columns, one row per monthly report, and save it as `data/cole/monthly-reports.csv`:

`month, institution, deaths, to_rush, to_hahnemann, to_northwestern_dental, other_schools, buried, claimed_by_family, seq, printed_page`

Fill in `printed_page` by hand from the scan on HathiTrust, so you can cite each report.

Once the file exists, this chunk charts where the bodies went. Delete `#| eval: false` and run it:

```{r}
#| label: monthly-reports-chart
#| eval: false

reports_file <- file.path(datadir, "monthly-reports.csv")  # the table you type up from those pages

if (file.exists(reports_file)) {  # only runs once you've made the file
  reports <- read_csv(reports_file)  # read it in

  reports %>%
    # turn the six disposition columns into two: disposition and number of bodies
    pivot_longer(c(to_rush, to_hahnemann, to_northwestern_dental, other_schools,
                   buried, claimed_by_family),
                 names_to = "disposition", values_to = "bodies") %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = month, y = bodies, fill = disposition)) +  # months across, one color per disposition
    geom_col() +  # stacked bars: total bodies per month
    facet_wrap(~ institution, ncol = 1) +  # one panel per institution
    labs(title = "Disposition of bodies, by month",
         x = NULL, y = "Bodies", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))  # tilt the month labels
} else {
  message("No monthly-reports.csv yet. This section is optional.")
}
```

Remember the context: an Illinois law of 1885 governed the transfer of unclaimed bodies to medical schools, so these numbers record a practice that was legally new. Who counted as "unclaimed"? Write down any observations or thoughts you might have now:
